explicit_validation.explanation: Paper explicitly compares GPT-4o judgments with human direct assessment scores on the same set of translations into African languages, noting inconsistencies and focusing on human evaluation due to reliability concerns

prompts.notes: Full prompts provided in Appendix B.5 for fluency, accuracy, and cohesion evaluation with detailed instructions and output formats

guidelines.notes: Used error span annotation (ESA) protocol within Appraise Evaluation Framework, with annotators marking spans and rating overall quality on 0-100 scale

sample_size.validated_by_both: 30 documents shared among all three annotators plus complete model outputs for selected languages
sample_size.notes: Limited to translations into four African languages (excluding Zulu) due to cost constraints, with focus on GPT-3.5, LLaMAX3-SFT1, and LLaMAX3-SFT10 models

validation_results.summary_finding: Human evaluation results aligned closely with d-chrF scores, while GPT-4o's judgments were inconsistent for translations into African languages, showing counterintuitive patterns such as low-fluency models having fewest errors

criteria_mapping.notes: LLM evaluated fluency, content errors, and cohesion errors with specific metrics, while humans used direct assessment scores and error span annotation; both methods assessed overall translation quality but with different scoring frameworks
